sections.hypothesis: After Binance lists a USDT-M perpetual on a coin that until then traded only spot, the coin underperforms the other coins over the next 30 days. If so, an altcoin portfolio should not hold a coin through its first month of perps (an exit rule, as the delisting study gave); a short version would be needs-shorting.
sections.rationale: Who pays: before a perp exists, pessimists can hardly bet against a small coin (spot borrowing is scarce), so its price reflects the optimists; a perp lets pessimists and hedgers in (Miller 1977, and Harrison and Kreps 1978: prices are too high when short selling is constrained). Selection adds to it: Binance lists perps on coins whose volume and attention have just risen, often after a run. Outside evidence: Bitcoin peaked the week CME futures launched in December 2017 and fell after, which the authors attribute to futures letting pessimists in (Hale, Krishnamurthy, Kudlyak and Shultz 2018, FRBSF Economic Letter 'How Futures Trading Changed Bitcoin Prices'; to check before freezing). Not a rejected family: an event, like the delisting study, not a chart pattern or a reversal. Suggested by an outside AI review (2026-11-18). Runs: one, a raw-effect study.
sections.rules: Events: each coin of the exploration half plus BTC, ETH and SOL (never the locked confirmation half) whose USDT-M perp (XUSDT, or 1000XUSDT) first settled funding on or after 2020-01-02 (Binance's funding archive starts 2020-01, so earlier listings are censored and left out), with at least 60 days of spot daily bars before that day, and the 30-day window ending before 2025-11-01 (no holdout data). Counted on 2026-11-18 before any return was read: 102 events (2020: 24, 2021: 18, 2022: 6, 2023: 33, 2024: 15, 2025: 6). Day 0 is the UTC day of the first funding settlement (the perp is known by day 0's close); returns run from day 1's open, as the delisting study's do. Abnormal return over a window = the coin's return minus the equal-weighted mean return of every other coin of the same universe that traded at both ends of the window. Primary window: day 1's open to day 31's open (30 days). Reported, deciding nothing: day -30 to day 0 (the run-up), day 1 to day 8 (the first week), and the share of events below zero. Events listed the same day are averaged into one; the bootstrap runs over listing days. Placebo: for each coin, 200 random days (seed 0) at least 60 days from its listing, the same window, giving a distribution of placebo mean abnormal returns.
sections.falsification: EXIT RULE (worth a rule in the altcoin portfolio's note) only if all hold: at least 50 listing days; the mean 30-day abnormal return is at most -3% (well above the cost of selling and buying back, about 0.5%); its bootstrap P(< 0) is at least 90% (5,000 resamples, seed 0); and it is below at least 90% of the placebo means (the effect is the listing, not the coin). INSUFFICIENT if fewer than 50 listing days. Otherwise KILL. Run once.
sections.parameters: Fixed before any return was read: 30-day primary window from day 1's open, 60 days of spot history, equal-weighted market adjustment, 200 placebo days a coin at least 60 days from the listing, 5,000 resamples, seed 0. No other window, universe or filter is tried; a change is a new version with a reason.
sections.costs: A measurement, not a strategy run: returns before costs. The bar of -3% is set against the cost of acting on it (selling a held coin and buying it back later: two taker fees of 7.5 bps and the coin's half-spread band twice, about 0.5% for a small coin). Not a trial (a raw-effect study), recorded in the findings.
